audio_caption: The audio clip begins with a male speaker stating that the lunar eclipse on September the 28th was surprisingly early, at least for him. Next, the same speaker mentions quickly connecting the camera module of his Raspberry Pi to a 100 to 300 mm zoom lens to capture that rare astronomical event. Following the speech is an animal sound, potentially a frog croaking.

A male speaker with a calm and informative tone describes how "the rear plastic cover of a lens has to be surface grounded and drilled with an 8 mm center hole." He then mentions that "the lens of the camera module has to be removed." The speaker proceeds to give instructions, stating: "put the camera board on a flat surface. I am using a piece of Teflon as bedding layer, and keep it in place with a caliper." He concludes the instructions, noting that "with a stick of cold, hot glue, you can press on the lens and unscrew it. You can also use a pencil with a rubber at the rear end." A brief, low sound is heard.

The clip starts with a male speaker advising the use of hot glue at the corners of boards to mount a camera module on a plastic cover. He explains the importance of flange focal distance, suggesting a 20 mm spacing, and acknowledges it's not perfect. But it's a solution he found for a certain event. The audio then fades into a musical interlude, a single sustained note, that serves as a brief, jarring contrast before concluding.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker stating his reasonably priced tripod is not a good solution for astronomical observations, emphasizing that you get enormous clearance for your money. Then, a low-frequency sound, possibly related to a dropping or impacting object, is heard.

The clip begins with speech from a male speaker, mentioning that "the Raspberry camera can't control the aperture of the lens." He explains how an aperture of less than four can be achieved by removing the lens while triggering it with "a special button." He adds that "the light sensor used with the Raspberry Pi camera module is clearly smaller than that of a standard camera the lens was manufactured for."

A male voice starts by explaining that a crop factor of approximately nine allows the focal length of a zoom lens to reach up to "2,700 mm". He then says they can get a total view of the moon by adjusting the zoom to approximately "130 mm", which equals "1,200 mm" with a Raspberry camera module.

The audio starts with speech by a male speaker with a slightly accented delivery, noting the difficulty of aiming a homemade telescope at the moon. He states that, "the result is surprisingly good," but, "it is not outstanding." The same speaker continues, observing the fast movement of celestial bodies and the inability of the cheap tripod to follow. Finally, the same voice says, "the lunar eclipse started at 7 minutes past 3 in the morning." The audio ends with a brief bit of music.

The audio begins with a male speaker posing a question about the movement of Earth's shadow. The speaker then transitions to explain that "the moon is not moving in a circular path around the earth". He continues explaining the distances between the moon and the earth and providing specific measurements. The audio then transitions to an "and" sound that is cut off, ending abruptly.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker mentioning a lunar eclipse recording and noting the Earth-Moon distance at the time. He adds that, on average, the space between Earth and the moon increases by about 3.8 centimeters each year. Then, the speaker says, "The moon is nippled by the Earth's umbra." The clip ends with the same speaker saying "The".

The audio clip features a single male speaker explaining details about recording sequences. He notes that the "second sequence was recorded at 15 minutes past 3". The speaker describes the image contrast as being too low, making it difficult to see the reddish part of the moon's surface shadowed by the earth. He continues discussing technical aspects, such as recording sequences with an aperture of 11 and an exposure time of 25 milliseconds using a software parameter called "shutter speed." Finally, the speaker notes that the light sensitivity was set to ISO 100 to reduce image noise.

The audio clip features a single male speaker with a clear, slightly formal tone, describing a sequence of events involving the moon, stating it was recorded at "22 minutes to 4 in the morning." He continues by noting that "after approximately 30 minutes, more than half of the Moon is covered by the Earth's umbra" and then explains that the following sequences are "wiggly" because he opened a window to follow the movement of the moon, and "warm air escapes through the opened window causing those optical distortions."

The audio begins with a male speaker providing facts about the moon's orbit and mass relative to Earth, speaking in a neutral, informative tone. He continues, summarizing an observation about the shape of the illuminated moon surface being reduced to a crescent, admitting failure to record the moon surface in the Earth's umbra, and concluding that he needs to upgrade his equipment for the next lunar eclipse. This is followed by a short, sci-fi-esque sound effect.

The audio clip begins with a speaker stating "At 6 minutes past 4, just a small fraction of the moon surface is still outside the Earth's umbra", suggesting an astronomical event. Shortly after, the same speaker is heard again saying, "At 24 minutes past 5, the moon starts leaving the umbra". This is followed by the same voice noting that "the celestial object is above the roofs of my small hometown from my point of view."

The audio clip begins with a male speaker describing atmospheric changes during a lunar eclipse, including temperature drops, convection, and the position of the moon in the sky. The speaker then notes the visibility of the moon's scintillation. The speaker mentions the observation point and time zone. The clip ends with another male speaker saying "End".

A male speaker begins by stating that "ten minutes past six" more than half of the moon's surface is visible. Then, there is mention that a passenger jet crossed the line of sight between the speaker and the moon. The speaker notes that Frankfurt Airport is just 80 km away and the jet is not climbing, but moving horizontally. He describes adjusting his telescope on the tripod so the moon moves horizontally through the screen to capture long video sequences. The speaker acknowledges the difficulty in adjusting the tripod and tracking the moon and mentions the moon's vertical movement toward the Earth's horizon. Concluding, the speaker notes that he can see the Earth's shadow on the bottom right of the moon.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker stating, "At 20 minutes past 6, the last but one sequence was recorded." He continues in a hopeful tone, mentioning it's his "first attempt ever to record the moon" and that he will "try to improve" his equipment for future recordings, hopefully "with better results". He then talks about the next lunar eclipse visible from his hometown in 2018. Following this, the speaker continues speaking, stating, "The last sequence was recorded at 26 minutes past 6," and announces, "The moon leaves the Umbra." before declaring, "the eclipse ended at 27 minutes past 6." The speaker then says, "You can get the build instruction of my telescope on the project page" and concludes the audio clip with a "Thanks for watching, and I'll be back."
